introduction-escaping-the-monolith.core: A single state file that grew to hundreds of resources makes every plan slow (Terraform refreshes everything), puts the entire estate in every change's blast radius, and serialises all teams on one lock. Escaping the monolith means splitting state into smaller stacks with clear dependency order, then moving resources between states without recreating them.

first_principles.problem: A 500-resource state takes 15 minutes to plan, and an app change risks touching the VPC.
truths: Plan time scales with resources refreshed.
derivation: Move resources with **state mv / removed + import**.

analogy.title: Splitting one huge warehouse into specialised depots
analogy.story: Finding anything in one giant warehouse takes forever; depots by category are faster, and a fire in one doesn't burn the rest.
analogy.breaks: Moving stock is physical; moving state is metadata but still risky.

example.title: Quick stats

code.text:
terraform state list | wc -l          # 512
time terraform plan -refresh=true     # real 14m52s
terraform state list | cut -d. -f1-2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

example.outcome: a case and map for splitting.

check.q: Why does plan time grow with state size?
check.a: Terraform refreshes every resource in state by calling cloud APIs before diffing.

strategy-the-stack-hierarchy.core: Split stacks form a dependency graph: apps need databases, databases need subnets, subnets need a VPC. Arrange them in a strict hierarchy where outputs flow only downward, from lower and more stable layers to higher and more volatile ones. Apply in topological order, and never let a lower layer read from a higher one.

first_principles.problem: After splitting, nobody knows which stack to apply first, and a new environment takes days to bring up.

analogy.title: Building floors bottom-up
analogy.story: You pour the foundation before walls and walls before the roof; the roof never supports the foundation.
analogy.breaks: Buildings aren't rebuilt weekly; stacks are re-applied constantly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: New environment in one ordered run.

check.q: Why must lower layers never depend on higher ones?
check.a: It would create cycles and make stable foundations change whenever volatile apps change, breaking the apply order.

resolving-state-hell-circular-dependenci.core: Circular dependencies appear when stack A needs B's output and B needs A's. A typical case: the app needs the DB endpoint, and the DB's security group needs the app's security group ID. Break the cycle by extracting the shared piece into a lower layer (create both security groups in a shared stack), by relying on stable identifiers such as tags or names instead of outputs, or by splitting a resource from its attachment.

first_principles.problem: App and DB stacks each wait for the other's output, so neither can be applied first.
truths: Attachments can be separated from resources.
derivation: **Extract** shared resources to a lower layer.

analogy.title: Two people each waiting for the other to call
analogy.story: Break it by agreeing on a meeting place in advance (shared layer) instead of waiting on each other.
analogy.breaks: People can improvise; Terraform simply errors or deadlocks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: App and DB stacks both consume SG IDs from below.

check.q: What's the most common fix for a cross-stack security-group cycle?
check.a: Create both security groups (and the rule linking them) in a shared lower stack that both upper stacks consume.

state-migration-during-re-platforming.core: Sometimes state is too messy for surgical `state mv`, for example old 0.12-era code with inconsistent naming. Then do a clean-room migration: write fresh, idiomatic code, use `removed { lifecycle { destroy = false } }` (or state rm) to drop resources from the old state without destroying them, adopt them into the new state with import blocks, and verify zero-diff plans on both sides before deleting old code.

first_principles.problem: A legacy monolith with hundreds of hand-imported resources must move to a new modular layout without downtime.
truths: Resources can leave state without being destroyed.
Two states must never manage one object.
derivation: **Remove** from old state with destroy = false.

analogy.title: Moving house with labelled boxes
analogy.story: You register items at the new house before crossing them off the old inventory, never leaving anything unclaimed or claimed twice.
analogy.breaks: Furniture can't be in two places; resources can be in two states, which is dangerous.

check.q: What must you avoid during state migration between stacks?
check.a: Having both stacks manage the same resource at once, which leads to conflicting changes or accidental destruction.
